focus: Identify adjacent routing judgments and define the evidence, serving, cost, fallback, and privacy requirements for default-on track narrowing.
noveltyJustification: This iteration moves from scorer changes and evaluation design to adjacent skill-hub routing, retrieval boundaries, actual hook constraints, release controls, and cost/privacy unknowns.
keyQuestions: Which other .skilled routing or classification decisions could benefit from measured judging?
What controls, cost, fallback, and risks would default-on integration require?
answeredQuestions: Which other .skilled routing or classification decisions could benefit from measured judging?
What controls, cost, fallback, and risks would default-on integration require?

keyFindings.title: The skill advisor’s near-tie route is the strongest adjacent candidate
keyFindings.summary: The skill advisor routes among skill hubs and has an offline near-tie Jev evaluator. Its documented holdout top-1 is 53/70; the default evaluator is zero-call and the Jev arm is explicitly gated. The existing number motivates testing but does not show that Jev improves it.

keyFindings.title: Jev can choose a spec track, but cannot repair a retrieval miss inside it
keyFindings.summary: Feature 017 defines Jev as a track chooser and leaves within-track retrieval and reranking outside scope. The trigger-index lookup returns no candidates when the query has no qualifying tokens. Treat track-selection errors separately from index/document-recall errors.

keyFindings.title: A default-on hook needs a fail-open contract and a bounded request path
keyFindings.summary: Existing skill-advisor hooks proceed on timeout/failure/no route, have a kill switch, bound prompt input and avoid raw prompt persistence. Jev integration should stay within each runtime budget and use broad retrieval for low confidence, none, unsupported input, missing binary/auth, timeout or invalid output. Jev serving is unimplemented and unmeasured.

keyFindings.title: Keep the current arm offline until an independent request holdout supports safe narrowing
keyFindings.summary: Feature 017 defers serving. Jev exact-track accuracy is 97/256 (37.9%) versus ripgrep 68/256 (26.6%), so relative significance does not prove it safe to hide results behind narrower search. Require a real frozen holdout, absolute accuracy and per-track recall criteria, calibrated abstention, shadow comparison, canary and kill switch; choose thresholds from product loss tolerance.

keyFindings.title: The current evidence prices benchmark work in calls, tokens, and subprocess time, not dollars or serving volume
keyFindings.summary: The run has 811 calls (810 choice calls across test rows/probes plus auth), 905,891 estimated input tokens, and per-class Jev subprocess timings. One serving choice would use a third as many choice calls as the three-order test arm per ambiguous request, but request volume, ambiguity rate, per-request token mix, pricing, cold-start, and end-to-end latency are unknown. Dollar cost was explicitly out of scope.

keyFindings.title: Minimize prompt disclosure and version drift at the Jev boundary
keyFindings.summary: The experiment sends the question text, fixed instruction and track options, not source files or paths unless included in the question. Keep prompts out of durable telemetry, minimize/redact, use a protected digest for reproducibility, pin versions and verify backend retention/network and billing terms before default-on.
